## Why It Matters {.center}


Many classification failures aren't model failures, they're **data** failures.

::: {.fragment}
Imbalance, noisy labels, hidden shortcuts, leakage, wrong tensor assumptions.
:::


# Image Representations


## Images as Tensors

::: {#fig-iad-tensor-anatomy}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}tensor_anatomy.png){width=55%}

An image as a tensor of shape **H × W × C**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Pixel values: `uint8 [0, 255]` → float `[0, 1]` → standardized (zero mean, unit variance)
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Shape conventions:**

- NumPy / PIL: `(H, W, C)` — *channels last*
- PyTorch: `(C, H, W)` — *channels first*

Mismatched conventions → silent bugs.
:::


## Channels: What Does C Mean?

::: {#fig-iad-rgb-vs-grayscale}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}rgb_vs_grayscale.png){width=55%}

RGB (3 channels) vs. grayscale (1 channel).
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **1**: grayscale, depth, IR/thermal, X-ray, ultrasound
- **3**: RGB (or HSV, same info, different axes)
- **4**: RGBA (alpha) or RGB + near-IR
- **N (10s–100s)**: multispectral / hyperspectral (remote sensing, agriculture, astronomy)
:::

::: {.fragment}
For ordinary 2-D images, only **C** changes , the tensor structure stays H × W × C.
For volumes or time series, we add additional axes.
:::

## Thermal Imaging

::: {#fig-iad-thermal-imaging}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}thermal_drone.gif){width=55%}

Thermal images are often single-channel sensor measurements: each pixel represents heat / infrared intensity.
For display, they may be mapped to false-color RGB.
:::



## Quiz: Batch Shape

A batch of **32** RGB images, each **224 × 224**, in PyTorch.

What is the tensor shape?

::: {.fragment}
**Answer:** `(32, 3, 224, 224)` — batch × channels × height × width
:::

::: {.fragment}
The batch dimension is always **first** in PyTorch, enables parallel GPU computation.
:::



## Resolution

::: {#fig-iad-resolution}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}resolution_comparison.png)

Same image at 224 × 224, 64 × 64, 16 × 16. Detail is progressively lost.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Higher** → detail, more memory + compute
- **Lower** → faster, but discards information
- **Aspect-ratio distortion** → squashing deforms objects
:::

::: {.fragment}
Common: resize shortest edge + center-crop, or resize with padding.
:::

## Label Noise

::: {#fig-iad-label-ambiguity}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}label_ambiguity.png){width=55%}

Wolf or large dog? Empty, or a tail at the edge of the frame?
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Inter-annotator disagreement** on borderline cases
- **Systematic errors**: annotators consistently confuse two classes
- **Ambiguous category boundaries**: class definitions overlap
:::

::: {.fragment}
Deep networks can eventually memorize noisy labels [@arpit_closer_2017], so validation monitoring and data inspection matter.
:::

## Hidden Bias

::: {#fig-iad-dataset-bias}
![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}dataset_bias.png){width=70%}

Same animal, different background: different prediction. The **background**, not the cow, drives the prediction. Adapted from @Beery2018.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Geographic**: limited regional diversity (architecture, vegetation, clothing)
- **Selection**:internet-sourced images overrepresent certain demographics/styles
- **Watermark / source artifacts**: visual quirks correlate with labels
:::



## Dataset Splits

::: {.incremental}
- **Train**: used to fit model parameters
- **Validation**: used for model selection and tuning
- **Test**: used once for final evaluation
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Splitting strategy** must match the data-generating process.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Random**: not always appropriate
- **Stratified**: preserve class distribution across splits
- **Grouped**: keep related images (same event, patient, location) in the same split
:::

## Data Leakage {.center}

Data leakage means the model receives information during training that would not be available at deployment.

Result: validation/test metrics look good, but real-world performance collapses.

::: {.incremental}
- **Near-duplicates** across splits (camera-trap bursts, video frames)
- **Same subject / location** in multiple splits
- **Preprocessing stats** computed over the *full* dataset (not just training)
:::








## Quiz: Skin Cancer Detection Dataset

500 patients, multiple visits each. Images randomly shuffled and split 80/10/10.

What goes wrong?

::: {.fragment}
The same patient can appear in both train and test.
The model may learn patient-specific cues instead of lesion-specific cues.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Fix:** split at the **patient** level.
:::


# Summary {.center}


## Key Takeaways

::: {.incremental}
- Images are tensors: usually H × W × C, but volumes/time series add axes.
- Shape conventions matter: NumPy/PIL use H × W × C; PyTorch uses C × H × W.
- Resolution is a trade-off between detail, memory, and compute.
- Dataset quality matters: imbalance, noisy labels, hidden bias, and leakage can dominate performance.
- Splits must respect the data structure: group related samples together.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**The model can only be as good as the data it learns from.**
:::
